name: layer-supertype
intent: Give every object in a layer one declared supertype that carries the behavior the layer shares - identity, versioning, audit and lifecycle rules - so that behavior has a single home and clients, mappers and frameworks can depend on one type.
problem: Every class in a layer independently needs the same small surface - identity, version or timestamp fields, audit hooks, equality, lifecycle callbacks - and without a shared home that behavior is copied into each class, or parked in a utility class callers must remember to use; the layer then has no single declared type that clients, mappers and test scaffolding can rely on, and the copies drift apart.
context: An application with recognisable layers (domain, mapping/persistence, presentation, service) whose members genuinely share state or behavior, and where infrastructure can key on a common type: an object-relational mapper assuming id accessors, a controller framework assuming rendering helpers, a test suite assuming fixtures, a registry assuming a lookup contract. Fowler notes the move is usually made automatically once a layer has common features; it costs the strongest coupling in object-oriented design, so it pays only where the shared surface is stable and the layer's members are meant to be treated uniformly.
benefits: The behavior every member of the layer needs (identity, version fields, timestamps, audit and lifecycle hooks, equality by identity) has exactly one home instead of being copied into each class or left to callers.
The layer acquires a declared type: clients, mappers, repositories, controllers and test scaffolding can be written against the supertype and work uniformly with every member.
Framework integration becomes a single decision: infrastructure can assume the shared members exist - a mapper relies on id accessors, an ORM maps the base's fields into every subclass table.
Cross-cutting layer policy (validation, logging, security checks, invariant enforcement) is applied once, in the base, instead of per class.
Adding a member to the layer is cheap: it inherits the common surface and supplies only what is specific to it, and new shared behavior is added with a single edit (pull-up refactoring has a target).
tradeoffs: Inheritance is the strongest coupling in object-oriented design: every layer member now depends on the base's internals and assumptions, so a change to the base is a change to the whole layer - the fragile base class problem - and the base must either be designed and documented for extension or sealed.

It consumes the single superclass slot in languages with single inheritance; later needs (a framework base, another layer's contract, value semantics) must then be met through interfaces, mixins or composition.
The base tends to accumulate whatever two members happen to share - helpers, constants, incidental state - until it is the layer's utility drawer rather than its contract.
It invites speculative generality: behavior is pulled up before a second concrete need exists, leaving abstract members and hooks that no member uses and hierarchies deeper than the domain.
Protected state and hooks widen the subclass contract: everything the base exposes to its subclasses becomes part of the API, and tightening it later breaks every member.

Uniform treatment through the base type can conflict with value-oriented or framework-driven designs (immutability, structural equality, no-arg constructors for ORMs), forcing annotations or workarounds per language.

participants.responsibility: Abstract type declaring the layer's shared contract: holds the state established at creation, implements the behavior every member shares, and declares the operations each member must supply.
Derives from the supertype, inherits the shared state and behavior, implements only what is specific to it, and is usable wherever the supertype is expected.
Code that works against the supertype alone - invoking shared operations and dispatching to member-specific ones - without naming concrete layer types.
Mapping, persistence, presentation or test machinery that relies on the common supertype to treat every layer member uniformly (id accessors, mapped fields, lifecycle hooks).

use_cases: A domain layer whose entities share identity, version and audit fields: a DomainObject supertype carrying the Identity Field and its accessors (Fowler's own example).
An ORM-mapped persistence layer where every entity inherits shared persistent state (@MappedSuperclass, Django abstract Meta models, ActiveRecord::Base-style bases) so the mapper can assume it.
A data-mapping layer where every mapper inherits an AbstractMapper providing the common lookup, registry and column-mapping mechanics.
Presentation layers: a base controller or presenter supplying rendering helpers, validation and error translation to every endpoint or screen class.
A service or infrastructure layer where every member shares transaction handling, tracing or retry policy, so the policy is applied once.
Test scaffolding for a layer: a base test case providing fixtures and lifecycle for all tests of that layer.

Hibernate/JPA persistence layer: a @MappedSuperclass base entity declaring @Id, @Version, and @CreatedDate fields so every concrete @Entity inherits them without duplication; ORM maps the base's fields into each subclass table.

Django model layer: an abstract Model base class (Meta.abstract=True) carrying created_at, updated_at and a custom primary key type (UUID), so every app model inherits consistent timestamps and key semantics without a shared table.

Spring Data JPA domain layer: an AbstractAuditable base providing @CreatedBy, @LastModifiedBy, @CreatedDate, @LastModifiedDate, enabled via @EnableJpaAuditing and consumed uniformly by all repository-backed entities.
Event-sourced domain layer: a base aggregate root declaring id, version and apply(Event) template method so every aggregate implements event sourcing conventions uniformly.

Microservice cross-cutting layer: a base command/query handler class supplying OpenTelemetry tracing spans, retry policy and correlation-id propagation to every endpoint without duplicating interceptor boilerplate.
GraphQL resolver layer: a base resolver class providing DataLoader caching, auth context extraction and field-level permission checks to every resolver method.
Batch-processing layer: a base Step implementation supplying retry template, skip policy and chunk-level monitoring to every ETL step.

Ruby on Rails model layer: Rails generates ApplicationRecord as the base for Active Record models, so each model inherits the framework's shared persistence and query behavior while app-specific model classes remain thin.
Laravel Eloquent model layer: application models extend Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Model, inheriting common ORM persistence, attribute and relationship behavior from one framework base.
ASP.NET Core API presentation layer: controllers derive from ControllerBase to share action-result helpers, request context and model-state behavior while each endpoint supplies its own actions.
avoid_when: The shared surface is only a marker with no behavior or state: declare an interface (Marker Interface) instead of spending the superclass slot.
The duplication is a single concern (logging, validation, caching) that only some members need: use a decorator, mixin or composition, which does not smear that concern over the whole layer.

Fewer than about three members actually share the behavior, or the sharing is anticipated rather than observed: wait until the duplication is real - Extract Superclass is a refactoring, not a prediction.
The layer's members must evolve or deploy independently: a shared base in a library creates lockstep releases; prefer Separated Interface plus composition.
The type would carry another layer's concerns (persistence in a domain base, HTTP in a service base): keep the layer boundary and inject the dependency.
The language offers a lighter mechanism for the same purpose (trait defaults, protocol extensions, mixins, embedding) and no shared stored state is needed.
anti_patterns: God base class: the supertype becomes the layer's dumping ground for helpers, constants and state that are not part of the layer contract.
Inheritance for code reuse rather than for the layer's type: members extend the base only to borrow a method, coupling unrelated classes and inviting fragile-base-class breakage.
Speculative hierarchy: an abstract base with hooks and per-member operations introduced while a single member exists - abstraction without duplication.
Cross-layer base: a domain supertype that knows about tables, HTTP or transactions, dragging persistence or presentation concerns into the middle of the application.
Reinventing the framework's layer supertype: hand-rolled entity or controller scaffolding built beside the base class the framework already provides.
Leaky base: protected fields and public setters exposed to subclasses 'in case they are needed', turning every implementation detail into a contract.
design_principles: DRY: behavior every member of the layer owns is implemented once, in the supertype.
Design for extension, or prohibit it (Effective Java, item 17): an inheritable base must document its self-calls and protected surface, or be sealed.
Liskov substitution: any layer member must be usable wherever the supertype is expected, so the base may promise only what every member can honor.
Prefer composition over inheritance for reuse; reserve inheritance for declaring the layer's type (is-a), not for borrowing code (has-a).
Single responsibility: the supertype owns the layer's shared contract, not unrelated utilities.
best_practices: Admit a member to the supertype only when every object in the layer needs it; keep the base abstract and minimal.
Make the base abstract with a protected constructor so it can never be instantiated, and establish the shared state there.
Never call overridable members from constructors or creation hooks; use template methods with documented extension points instead.
Keep state private and expose protected hooks deliberately; protected mutable fields are a contract that cannot be tightened later.
Prefer final/sealed members for invariants and abstract members for required behavior, so subclasses cannot break the base's rules.
Name the base with the layer's vocabulary (DomainObject, AbstractMapper, ApplicationController), never Base/Helper/Util.

When the language cannot inherit, or the superclass slot must stay free, use the equivalent mechanism - trait defaults, protocol extension, mixin, embedded base struct - instead of duplicating the shared surface.
Expose auditing via framework annotations (@CreatedDate, @LastModifiedBy) rather than hand-rolled lifecycle hooks, so the behavior is tested and maintained by the framework team.
Use @MappedSuperclass (JPA), abstract Meta (Django) or @TypeDef (Hibernate) for shared column mappings - never rely on the ORM auto-mapping undefined columns, which varies by vendor.
Declare the id type generically (e.g., <PK extends Serializable> in Java, Optional[UUID] in Python) so consuming code is type-safe regardless of the concrete key strategy.
Override equals() and hashCode() using business key or id, never the whole object graph; a naive object equality implementation on a base class carrying lazy proxies will break Set/Dict operations.
For frameworks that require a no-arg constructor (JPA, various ORMs), keep it protected and chain it from the canonical constructor so subclasses cannot omit super() initialization.
Seal the base at the language level (sealed/final) unless extension is a deliberate, documented, tested policy - this eliminates the accidental subclass problem entirely.
When adding a new shared field, apply the Rule of Three: wait until a third class genuinely needs it before pulling it up; premature abstraction creates unused hooks.
Place framework-specific annotations only on the base class, never duplicated on every member; this keeps the annotation surface minimal and ensures the ORM processes them consistently.
sources: Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (Addison-Wesley, 2002) - Layer Supertype, ch. 18 'Base Patterns' (pp. 475-476), including the Domain Object example.

Hibernate ORM Documentation - @MappedSuperclass: inherit persistent attributes from a non-entity base class (https://github.com/hibernate/hibernate-orm/blob/main/documentation/src/main/asciidoc/introduction/Entities.adoc)

Django Documentation - Abstract base classes: share fields and Meta across models without creating a table for the base (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/db/models/#abstract-base-classes)

Spring Data JPA - AbstractAuditable<U, ID>: base entity class providing @CreatedBy, @LastModifiedBy, @CreatedDate, @LastModifiedDate auditing fields (https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-data-jpa/blob/main/src/main/java/org/springframework/data/jpa/domain/AbstractAuditable.java)

Spring Data JPA - AbstractPersistable<ID>: base entity class implementing Persistable with isNew() detection via @PostPersist/@PostLoad callbacks (https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-data-jpa/blob/main/src/main/antora/modules/ROOT/pages/jpa/entity-persistence.adoc)
Effective Java, 3rd Ed., Item 17: 'Design and document for inheritance or else prohibit it' - the authoritative treatment of base class design rules and the fragile base class problem.

JPA 2.2 API - @MappedSuperclass: mapping information is inherited by entity subclasses while the mapped superclass has no dedicated table (https://docs.hibernate.org/jpa/2.2/api/javax/persistence/MappedSuperclass.html)
Django Documentation - Models and abstract base classes: common fields and behavior are inherited without a table for the abstract base (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.1/topics/db/models/)
Spring Data JPA Documentation - AbstractAuditable is a convenience base for created/modified audit fields (https://docs.spring.io/spring-data/jpa/reference/auditing.html)
Ruby on Rails Guides - ApplicationRecord as the base class for Active Record models (https://guides.rubyonrails.org/active_record_basics.html)
Laravel API - Eloquent models extend Illuminate\\Database\\Eloquent\\Model (https://api.laravel.com/docs/13.x/Illuminate/Database/Eloquent/Model.html)
ASP.NET Core Web API Documentation - controllers derive from ControllerBase for common API behavior (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/web-api/?view=aspnetcore-9.0)
Empirical Software Engineering - Fragile base-class problem, problem? (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1007/s10664-016-9448-2)
